1.pericope_label: The book of the generations of Adam

schools.summary: Gill takes the chapter for Adam's descent through Seth to Noah, ten generations only, with nothing of Cain's line or the collateral branches. Calvin reads the title as a catalogue and states its purpose: to show that in the prodigious multitude of men there was always a number, however small, who worshipped God, preserved by celestial guardianship lest his name be obliterated and the seed of the Church fail. On the single name given to the first pair he finds a commendation of marriage, posterity learning to cherish the bond the more sacredly on seeing their first parents called by one name, and dismisses as trifling the Jewish inference that married persons are therefore called Adam.

Henry calls the phrase the title of the whole chapter, a catalogue not of all Adam's posterity but of the holy seed, the names and ages and deaths of those who succeeded the first Adam in the custody of the promise and were ancestors of the second. From the rehearsal of the creation he draws four lessons: that God made man, who is therefore not his own master, the Author of his being being also the centre of his motions; that there was a day on which he was made, so he is the junior of the creation; that he was made righteous and holy, and therefore happy; and that they were made male and female for mutual comfort as well as increase.

Clarke observes that the Hebrew rendered book means a register, any kind of writing, even a bill of divorce, and thinks the creation account is repeated here to keep man in mind of the glory from which he fell and to prove that the miseries and death of his present state came from his transgression and not his original condition; since the deaths of the patriarchs are now to be recited, it was necessary to preface them so, to justify the ways of God to man. Wesley follows Henry throughout and presses the fourth lesson further, that both were made immediately by God's hand and both in his likeness, so between the sexes there is not the inequality some imagine.

Ellicott takes the repetition to prove nearly the opposite of what Clarke draws from it: man is fallen, but the words recur to show the divine likeness was not lost, nor the blessing given at his creation revoked, since that likeness does not mainly consist in moral innocence and was untouched by sin except so far as sin corrupted the vessel holding the gift. Keil and Delitzsch note that the ages given here are withheld from the Cainite list, so this genealogy is at once a line of development and a chronology, the accursed family having no future history; and they mark the formula that now begins, ending each time in the words and he died, which by its constant recurrence shows that death reigned from Adam downward as an unchangeable law.

debates.question: Why is the creation account repeated here?

sides.position: to show what was lost — man was made free of natural and moral evil, so the death now to be recited came from his transgression
to show what was kept — the divine likeness was not lost by the fall, since it does not mainly consist in moral innocence

themes: this is the book of the generations of Adam
in the likeness of God made he him
the holy seed distinguished from Cain’s line
begat in his own likeness, after his image

schools.summary: Gill insists the years are solar, not lunar, against Varro, reckoning them at three hundred and sixty-five days and odd hours after the Egyptian usage of Moses's time, and argues from the absurdities of the alternative, that Enoch must else have begotten a son in his sixth year and the interval between creation and deluge shrink to two hundred years; he supports the long lives from heathen writers who say the ancients lived a thousand years, noting that Josephus appeals to Manetho and Berosus. Calvin dwells on what the overlapping lives allowed: through six successive ages the voice of Adam might daily resound among Seth's people, renewing the memory of the creation, the fall and the punishment, and testifying to the hope left after chastisement, since instruction from the mouth of the eyewitness was far more forcible than what his sons could hand on. On the closing words he denies that they are superfluous, since they warn us that death was not denounced in vain and that we lie under the curse unless deliverance is had elsewhere; it is useful in a picture of so many ages to see at one glance the continual course of divine vengeance, for otherwise we dream of an immortality on earth.

Wesley pushes the sentence back to its cause: in the day Adam ate the forbidden fruit he became mortal and began to die, so his whole life afterwards was a forfeited and condemned life, and more, a wasting and dying one; he was not merely like a criminal under sentence but like one already crucified, who dies slowly and by degrees.

Ellicott finds the numbers of the Bible involved in great difficulty, since Hebrew numeration attaches values to letters and the words so formed, being unmeaning, are easily corrupted; the three authorities differ widely on the interval from the expulsion out of Paradise to the flood, the Hebrew making it 1656 years, the Samaritan 1307 and the Greek 2262, while agreeing almost everywhere on the individual lives. He finds an appearance of untrustworthiness about the Greek calculations and ranks the Samaritan nearly equal with the Hebrew. Whatever the figures, he holds the Bible plainly represents life as vastly prolonged before the flood and rapidly shortening after, and teaches that in the Messianic age it shall be prolonged again, though he accepts the physiologists' verdict that man as he now is cannot pass a hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty years.

themes: all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years
and he died
were the years solar or lunar?
the patriarchs living together

schools.summary: Gill explains why only one son is ever named, since Enos was surely not Seth's firstborn and no doubt there were children before him, but he alone is named because the line ran through him from Adam to Noah, the father of the new world, from whom the Messiah was to spring, to give that descent being the principal view of the book. The rest of his notes are textual, marking where the Greek makes Enos a hundred and ninety at Cainan's birth and where the Samaritan reads only sixty-two for Jared, which Gill thinks can hardly have been the age at a first son.

Henry makes the silence of the record his subject, asking why so little is said at such length and answering that it might have been delivered in fewer words, but there is not one idle word in God's books, whatever there is in men's. He gives two reasons for the fullness: condescension to the meanest capacity, since the total is set down for those who could not add it themselves; and the pleasure God takes in his people's names, Cain's line being numbered in haste while this account of the holy seed is enlarged and given in words at length, so we are told how long those lived who lived in God's fear and when those died who died in his favour, while as for the rest it is no matter. The memory of the just is blessed, he closes, but the name of the wicked shall rot.

Wesley reproduces Henry's passage and adds a meditation on the length of the lives, that not one died before he had seen almost eight hundred years, which he calls a long while for an immortal soul to be imprisoned in a house of clay. Two inferences follow: the present life cannot have been the burden to them it commonly is now, or they would have grown weary of it, and the life to come was not revealed as clearly as under the gospel, or they would have been impatient to be gone. He will assign natural causes too, thinking it probable that before the flood the earth was more fruitful, the air more healthful and the influences of the heavenly bodies more benign.

Ellicott finds in the short intervals a proof about the calendar, that the years cannot have been revolutions of the moon since Enos was ninety at his son's birth, Cainan seventy and Mahalaleel sixty-five, though the supposition would sit better on the Greek text, where no patriarch has a son before his hundred and sixty-second year. On the name Jared he is cautious, reporting the derivation from a word for descent and the attempts to identify him with an Indian water-god, which competent modern commentators regard as exploded, and Sayce's Assyrian sense of servant, which does not satisfy him either; until that dialect is thoroughly explored he thinks we can scarcely speak with certainty about these names. He does infer from Jared's age at Enoch's birth that Enoch was probably not the eldest son but came into the birthright by his own excellencies.

themes: the formula repeated through five generations
why the record is so full
the length of the antediluvian lives
the name of Jared

schools.summary: Gill reads Methuselah's name as a prophecy, since on Bochart's derivation it means that when he dies there shall be a sending forth of waters to destroy the earth, and supposes Enoch had walked with God before this point but now more closely, holding on despite the apostasy that began in his father's days. Calvin sharpens the singularity by an objection: Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel and Jared were all living and their piety was celebrated a few verses earlier, so the age cannot have been barbarous with so many excellent teachers, from which he infers that the probity of the man whom the Spirit exempted from the common order was rare and almost singular. He draws the practical lesson that here is the way to escape the manners of those we live among, since public custom is a violent tempest and no contagion is worse than evil example; and on the ending he says a man must be shamelessly contentious who will not acknowledge something extraordinary, since all are taken out of the world by death while Moses declares that Enoch went by an unusual mode and was received miraculously, as Elijah afterwards was.

Henry marks the change of pace, the accounts having run on for generations with nothing to distinguish them but names and numbers, and then one not to be passed over: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, who excelled them all and was the brightest star of the patriarchal age. On what walking with God means he is fullest: it denotes true religion, for what is godliness but walking with God, and it presupposes reconciliation, since two cannot walk together except they be agreed; it is to set him always before us and act as men under his eye, to live in communion with him, and to make his word our rule and his glory our end.

Clarke goes to the words, finding that Enoch signifies to instruct or dedicate, from which he judges the man was early taught the things of God, and that the Hebrew verb stands in a form denoting what a man does upon himself, so Enoch set himself to walk, fixedly purposed not to receive the grace of God in vain. Wesley follows Henry almost word for word and adds that to walk with God is to comply with his will and be a worker together with him, taking it that Enoch grew eminent for piety only after Methuselah's birth.

Ellicott observes that the Greek renders the phrase Enoch pleased God, whence the testimony quoted in Hebrews, the Hebrew giving the cause of which the Greek names the effect. In place of the mournful refrain closing every other life here, there is an early removal into another world without pain or decay, suggesting that long life was not the highest blessing, so that one of Adam's posterity after the fall achieved what Adam in Paradise had failed to do; he adds that the removal fell about the middle of the antediluvian period and that Enoch's age was three hundred and sixty-five, the number of days in a year.

themes: Enoch walked with God
the name Methuselah as prophecy
and he was not, for God took him
walking with God against the current of the age

25.pericope_label: Methuselah, Lamech, and the naming of Noah

schools.summary: Gill gives the Jewish reason why no man reached a thousand years, that a thousand years is God's day and none may arrive at it, observes that Seth's line repeats names from Cain's, and joins the two senses of Noah's name, that rest gives comfort and comfort flows from rest. Calvin settles the philology against the first of them: the verb meaning to comfort does not answer to the noun meaning rest unless a letter be called superfluous, and the name comes from the latter, so Lamech's words are either a transmutation of letters or a bare allusion. He asks besides how a father could hope so much from a son whose disposition he could not yet have discerned, and answers with the Jews that the saying was a prophecy, faulting them only for restricting to agriculture what belongs to all human misery.

Henry takes Methuselah's name for a warning, since the longest liver who ever was carried death about in his name, and presses the moral of the age, that the longest liver must die at last and neither youth nor age discharges from that war. He enters a scruple worth noting, that the common account of these men presumes every patriarch named here was holy and good, which he is loth to deny yet does not see can be inferred merely from their enrolment among the ancestors of Christ. In the naming of Noah he hears both a complaint of the calamitous state of human life, our days being spent in labour on a cursed ground, and an expectation that carries more than a parent's ordinary wish, some prophecy probably lying behind it.

Clarke is cautious about the record of Methuselah's age, calling it the longest life mentioned in Scripture and probably the longest ever lived while denying we have authority to say so; yet he will not call life a misfortune, since uncertain and full of evils as it is, it is a blessing in all its periods if devoted to the glory of God and the interest of the soul. On the name Noah he separates the two roots and chooses rest over comfort, asking what is more comfortable than rest after toil, and reads the words prophetically of the man who built the ark, taking him for a typical person since after the waters dried God smelled a savour of rest. Wesley reproduces Henry on the name and on the death of the longest liver.

Ellicott adds the bleakest note in the chapter, that this is the first child since Eve's day recorded as named at birth, and that in both cases the name ended in disappointment, for Noah brought no rest and in his days came the flood.

debates.question: What does the name Noah mean?

sides.position: rest rather than comfort — and what is more comfortable than rest after toil?
rest, on philological grounds: the verb for comfort does not answer to the noun for rest unless a letter be called superfluous
both together, since rest gives comfort and comfort flows from rest

themes: Methuselah carried death in his name
the longest liver must die at last
this same shall comfort us
does Noah mean rest or comfort?

schools.summary: Gill can hardly think Noah lived so long childless and supposes he may have had children who died, though he reports the view that Providence ordered it so, an earlier start giving him more than the ark could hold; he works the dates out to make Japheth probably the eldest, since Ham was the younger and Shem was a hundred two years after the flood. Calvin dismisses the pious reading outright, holding that those err who find Noah's chastity proclaimed here, since the text neither says he was unmarried till then nor tells when he first became a father; Moses is naming the time he was warned of the deluge and adds that about then he was father of three sons, not that he had them already but because they were born not long after. He declines to say whether the earlier men in the list were firstborn, since Moses meant only to follow the succession of the Church, and observes that God, to keep men from a vain confidence in the flesh, often chooses those who come later in nature's order.

Clarke states the principle governing such lists, that where Scripture marks precedency the favoured son is put first though younger, as Jacob before Esau and Ephraim before Manasseh, and confesses he cannot account for Ham appearing out of his natural order at all. He closes the chapter by standing back from it, noting that of all these patriarchs the best was on earth the shortest time, Enoch's years being exactly the days of a solar revolution, and that Adam lived to see Lamech in the ninth generation, being the first who lived, the first who sinned and the first to taste death naturally, Abel's being violent. Wesley gives the reason for Shem's place, that the covenant was entailed on him and from him both Christ the head and the church the body descend, his very name meaning a name; and he explains why the old world's degeneracy is set down so fully before the story of its ruin, for the glory of God's justice and for warning to a wicked world.

Ellicott says flatly that no reason is given for Noah's late fatherhood, and that it does not follow he had no other sons, only that any such were unworthy to share the deliverance; he thinks it remarkable too that none of the three in the ark had children until after the flood. He glosses the three names as Shem, name or glory, the owner of the birthright and progenitor of our Lord; Ham, the dark-coloured, ancestor of the Egyptians and Cushites; and Japheth, the widener or on another account the fair, who though youngest fathered most of the races of Europe.

themes: Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth
why Noah was five hundred years old
the order of dignity, not of birth
the chapter looking forward to the flood
